1 --- 2 title: Running a relay 3 description: Stand up the PDS, check its health, and understand what you are responsible for. 4 --- 5 6 The PDS is a single Rust binary with a SQLite database. It is designed to be 7 easy to host — the whole point of the project. 8 9 ## Health 10 11 Every deployment exposes a health endpoint the platform can watch: 12 13 ```sh 14 curl -sS https://your-pds.example.com/xrpc/_health 15 ``` 16 17 A healthy server reports its version, derived from the workspace version — the 18 same source these docs stamp — so the server and its documentation cannot claim 19 different versions. 20 21 :::note[Status is stated, not colored] 22 The operator console reports raw facts — version, uptime, counts, sweep 23 last-runs — and draws no `healthy`/`degraded`/`down` verdict of its own: the 24 thresholds are the operator's judgment, not the API's shape. What is wrong is 25 made legible in place — a troubled background sweep carries a trailing `!` glyph 26 and a named fault beside its figures, never a bare colored dot. A degraded 27 server tells you _what_ degraded. 28 ::: 29 30 34 35 On a degraded relay, the same readout flags each troubled background sweep with 36 a trailing `!` glyph and a named fault. A sweep whose last completed pass keeps 37 ageing reads `stale` — passes have stopped completing, so the sweep is dead. One 38 that completed but skipped work reads `failed ` — it ran, yet recorded `n` 39 errors (for blob GC, an account whose reconcile failed is skipped, so its blobs 40 stay uncollected until the fault is fixed). The two are named so they read apart on a 41 row that has both, and _what_ degraded is legible without relying on color. 42 43 47 48 ## Is the upstream relay seeing you? 49 50 A healthy server that no relay is crawling is invisible to the network — and an 51 upstream relay can silently drop your subscription. The console's Home screen 52 carries a **Relay federation** block that compares your server's exact sequencer 53 head against what the upstream relay reports for your host: the relay's 54 lifecycle status, its cursor, how many events it is behind, and when it last 55 consumed one. **Request crawl** re-invites the relay on demand — the recovery 56 move when the readout says the relay has stopped listening. 57 58 62 63 The same facts are served at `GET /v1/admin/relay-status` and the re-invite at 64 `POST /v1/admin/request-crawl` — see the [API reference](/operator/reference/api/). 65 66 ## What you are responsible for 67 68 - **Durability** — the SQLite database is the identity store. Back it up. 69 Production streams continuous backups to object storage with Litestream — see 70 [Backups & restore](/operator/backups/). 71 - **Availability** — users' clients reach your server to read and write. Health 72 checks and restart policy are your safety net. 73 - **You can't lock anyone in** — you hold the lowest-precedence rotation key; 74 the user's device key (`rotationKeys[0]`) and their recovery key outrank it, 75 so they can move their identity to another server whenever they choose. Design 76 your operations for that. 77 78 :::caution[Do not treat the DB as disposable] 79 Losing the database is not like losing a cache. It holds the repositories your 80 users depend on. Verify your restore path before you need it. 81 ::: 82 83 ## Deploy 84 85 The server deploys as an OCI image (Railway builds the `Dockerfile` directly). 86 The full runbook — staging vs production branches, Litestream backups, and the 87 security posture — lives in the repository's `docs/deploy.md`. 88

1 --- 2 title: Moderation 3 description: Takedown, restore, credential revocation, and account repair from the operator console. 4 --- 5 6 The operator console (the "Brass Console" companion app) exposes the moderation 7 actions an operator needs. Every action reports exactly what it did — the console 8 does not soften or hide the effect. 9 10 ## Actions 11 12 16 17 On the **Moderation** screen (look up an account by DID first): 18 19 - **Takedown** — stop serving an account: logins, writes, and sync are refused 20 until it is restored. 21 - **Restore** — reverse a takedown (the account resumes serving unless it is also 22 suspended or deactivated). 23 - **Credential revocation** — the incident-response follow-up for a compromised 24 account: in one sweep it revokes the account's **sessions, app passwords, OAuth 25 grants and pending authorization codes, and transfer-device tokens**, and reports 26 the literal per-family counts. The account's **main password is untouched**, and 27 any already-issued access tokens lapse on their own within minutes. Every holder 28 — including the owner — is signed out and must log in again. 29 30 You reach an account by tapping it in the account list, which is searchable by 31 handle or DID and shows each account's blob quota. 32 33 37 38 On the **Account detail** screen (reached by tapping an account in the list): 39 40 - **Correct an email** — fix an account's email address; this resets it to 41 unconfirmed. 42 - **Issue a password-reset token** — mint a single-use, one-hour reset token for 43 out-of-band delivery. This is **refused for a passwordless / key-sovereign 44 account** — those recover through their escrowed key share, not a reset. 45 46 Both takedown and credential revocation are destructive, so the console arms them 47 behind a two-tap confirmation that restates the target, then a biometric gate, 48 before anything is signed. 49 50 :::caution[Takedown is server-scoped, not identity-scoped] 51 A takedown affects what _your_ server serves. Because the user holds 52 `rotationKeys[0]`, they can migrate their identity elsewhere. Moderation is your 53 control over your infrastructure, not custody over their identity — keep that 54 distinction clear when you communicate an action. 55 ::: 56 57 ## Labeler watching — flagged accounts 58 59 Custos can watch ATProto **labelers** (moderation services) and flag any hosted 60 account they label. Flagged accounts float to the top of the console's account 61 list with an explicit `⚑` indicator per label — the label value, the labeler, 62 and when it was applied — and the Home screen shows a flagged-accounts notice 63 for the active server. This turns the account list from a neutral roster into a 64 spam/abuse triage view: if a labeler your network trusts flags one of your 65 accounts, you see it on your next glance at the console. 66 67 Watching is **off by default** — you choose which labelers' judgment reorders 68 your console. The recommended starting point is Bluesky's moderation service: 69 70 ```bash 71 # Environment form: comma-separated labeler DIDs, each watching every label value. 72 EZPDS_LABELER_WATCHED=did:plc:ar7c4by46qjdydhdevvrndac 73 ``` 74 75 or, in `pds.toml`, with an optional per-labeler watchlist (empty or omitted 76 `labels` means every label from that labeler counts): 77 78 ```toml 79 [labeler] 80 poll_interval_secs = 900 # default: 15 minutes 81 82 [[labeler.watched]] 83 did = "did:plc:ar7c4by46qjdydhdevvrndac" # Bluesky Moderation 84 labels = ["spam", "!hide", "!warn"] # omit to watch every label 85 86 [[labeler.watched]] 87 did = "did:web:some-other-labeler.example" # any labeler works, not just Bluesky's 88 ``` 89 90 How it works: a background pass polls each watched labeler's 91 `com.atproto.label.queryLabels` for your hosted accounts (the labeler's query 92 endpoint is resolved from its DID document), honoring label negations and 93 expiry, and reconciles the flagged state the console reads. The first pass runs 94 at startup, then every `poll_interval_secs`. The health readout reports the 95 watcher's last completed pass, so a stale pass is visible on the Status screen. 96 97 Two things worth knowing before you enable it: 98 99 - **Each poll discloses your hosted-account DIDs to the watched labeler** (they 100 arrive as the query's `uriPatterns`). Hosted DIDs are already publicly 101 enumerable via `com.atproto.sync.listRepos`, but watching a labeler does 102 establish a recurring outbound relationship with it — which is why this is an 103 explicit opt-in rather than a default. 104 - **A flag is the labeler's opinion, not a verdict.** Flagging changes only the 105 sort order and the indicator; it takes no action against the account. Takedown 106 and credential revocation remain your deliberate, gated decisions above. 107 108 Removing a labeler from the config (or disabling watching entirely) clears its 109 flags on the next pass or restart — flagged state never outlives the 110 configuration that produced it. 111 112 ## Accountability 113 114 Moderation actions are shown with their subject, the operator device that signed 115 them, and the result — status carried in text, not by color alone. Pair any 116 externally visible action with a clear, honest explanation to the affected user; 117 the tooling reports the literal truth, and so should you. 118 119 :::note[Per-device operator keys] 120 Operator actions are signed by a per-device key (Secure-Enclave-backed on real 121 devices). Revoking a device revokes its ability to act, per relay, without 122 disturbing the others. 123 ::: 124

2	title: Backups & restore
3	description: Continuous SQLite backups with Litestream, blob replication with the bucket mirror, integrity scrubbing, and how to restore.
4	---
5	
6	The PDS keeps its records in one SQLite database and its blobs (media files) on
7	the volume next to it, so backing those two things up **is** your
8	disaster-recovery plan. Custos uses [Litestream](https://litestream.io/) to
9	stream the database to object storage continuously and restore it on boot, and
10	its own **blob mirror** to do the same for blob files.
11	
12	## How it works
13	
14	When the Litestream environment variables are set, the container runs the PDS
15	under Litestream: it streams the SQLite write-ahead log to your bucket as writes
16	happen (not a nightly snapshot — a continuous replica), and on boot it restores
17	from that replica if the local database is missing. So a current restore point
18	always exists.
19	
20	The replica is defined in `litestream.yml` (committed in the repo) with
21	`force-path-style: false` — virtual-hosted-style addressing, which
22	Railway/Tigris-style buckets require.
23	
24	## Turning it on
25	
26	Set these on the environment you want backed up (production; staging and local
27	leave them unset and run the PDS directly):
28	
29	| Variable | Role |
30	| --- | --- |
31	| `LITESTREAM_S3_BUCKET` | The bucket the replica is written to. Setting this is what switches Litestream on. |
32	| `LITESTREAM_S3_ENDPOINT` | Object-storage endpoint (e.g. your Tigris/S3-compatible host). |
33	| `LITESTREAM_ACCESS_KEY_ID` | Access key for the bucket. |
34	| `LITESTREAM_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` | Secret key for the bucket. |
35	
36	:::caution[The bucket credentials are secrets]
37	Store them in your platform's secret manager, never in the repository or the
38	image — the same discipline as the [master key](/operator/configuration/). Anyone
39	with the replica has a full copy of your accounts' data.
40	:::
41	
42	:::caution[The replica is only half the picture]
43	This backup protects the *ciphertext*. It does **not** protect the
44	[master key](/operator/configuration/) that decrypts it — back that up
45	separately, in a different store than this replica. If the key is ever lost
46	or compromised, follow the [master-key disaster runbook](/operator/master-key-runbook/)
47	instead of restoring from here alone.
48	:::
49	
50	## Blobs: the bucket mirror
51	
52	Litestream replicates only the SQLite database. Uploaded blobs — avatars,
53	post images, video — live as files on the deployment volume, where losing the
54	volume would destroy every account's media. The blob mirror is the Litestream
55	analogue for those files: a periodic sweep uploads every stored blob to an
56	S3-compatible bucket, and on boot the server attempts to restore any file
57	missing from the volume out of the bucket **before it takes traffic**. The
58	restore is best-effort per blob: a blob whose bytes exist in neither place, or
59	whose bucket copy fails content-hash verification, is logged loudly (per-CID
60	error plus a boot summary count) and boot continues — that blob stays
61	unavailable rather than blocking startup.
62	
63	Turn it on by setting a bucket (unset means disabled):
64	
65	| Variable | Role |
66	| --- | --- |
67	| `EZPDS_BLOB_MIRROR_BUCKET` | Bucket the mirror writes to. Setting this is what switches the mirror on. |
68	| `EZPDS_BLOB_MIRROR_ENDPOINT` | S3-compatible endpoint URL. |
69	| `EZPDS_BLOB_MIRROR_ACCESS_KEY_ID` | Access key for the bucket. |
70	| `EZPDS_BLOB_MIRROR_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` | Secret key for the bucket. |
71	
72	The sweep also propagates deletions, on a lag: after blob garbage collection or
73	account deletion removes a blob's database row, a subsequent sweep deletes the
74	bucket object, so the mirror tracks the live blobstore rather than growing
75	forever (the worst case of the lag is the bucket briefly retaining collected
76	blobs). As a tripwire against acting on a wrong or empty database, a sweep that
77	finds no blob rows at all while the bucket has objects skips delete propagation
78	entirely. The full knob list (region, path-style addressing,
79	key prefix, sweep interval) is in the
80	[configuration reference](/operator/reference/config/).
81	
82	:::note[Same discipline as the database replica]
83	Blob bytes are content-addressed but they are still your users' data — keep the
84	mirror bucket's credentials in your secret manager, exactly like the Litestream
85	bucket's.
86	:::
87	
88	## Blob integrity: the scrub sweep
89	
90	A backup only helps if the bytes it protects are still good. A periodic **scrub
91	sweep** re-hashes every stored blob against its recorded CID and size, and walks
92	the blob directory for orphans in both directions — a database row whose file has
93	gone missing, and a file that no row owns. Bitrot, a truncated write, or a bad
94	restore surfaces as an operator alarm (the `blob_scrub_*` metrics and
95	`GET /v1/admin/health`) **months before a migration would trip over it**, rather
96	than as a mystery at the worst possible moment.
97	
98	When the [bucket mirror](#blobs-the-bucket-mirror) is configured, the sweep can
99	do more than report: a file that fails its hash or has gone missing is
100	**auto-healed** from the mirror's verified-good copy. Auto-heal is on by default
101	and has no effect when the mirror is disabled — with no verified copy to pull
102	from, a bad file is only ever flagged, never silently replaced. Both knobs
103	(`blob_scrub.interval_secs`, default 6 hours; `blob_scrub.auto_heal`) are in the
104	[configuration reference](/operator/reference/config/).
105	
106	Two guarantees close the loop around the sweep, so it catches genuine bitrot
107	rather than gaps the write and read paths should have handled themselves:
108	
109	- **Writes are crash-durable.** An uploaded blob is written to a temp file,
110	  fsynced, atomically renamed onto its content-addressed path, and the directory
111	  fsynced, *before* the database row is recorded. A crash or power loss can no
112	  longer leave truncated bytes at a valid path behind a row that already
113	  committed.
114	- **Reads are verified.** `getBlob` re-hashes a blob against its CID before
115	  serving it and returns a 404 (flagging the scrub alarm counter) on a mismatch,
116	  so a corrupted file is never handed to a downstream cache. A verified response
117	  carries the long-lived `immutable` cache header the blob spec recommends.
118	
119	## Restoring
120	
121	To restore the database from the replica:
122	
123	```sh
124	litestream restore <path-to-db>
125	```
126	
127	Litestream pulls the latest state (or a point in time) from the bucket. On a
128	fresh container the PDS does this automatically on boot when the local database is
129	absent.
130	
131	### Rollback after a bad release
132	
133	Schema migrations are **forward-only** — there is no down-path. Redeploying an
134	earlier `vX.Y.Z` tag is safe **only** when the schema change was
135	backward-compatible. If it wasn't, roll back by restoring the database from the
136	Litestream replica to a point *before* the promote, rather than by redeploying
137	old code against a newer schema.
138	
139	:::note[Inspect without rolling back]
140	To look inside the replica without touching production, restore a throwaway copy
141	and query it with `sqlite3` — no rollback required. The repository's operator
142	debug kit documents this runbook.
143	:::
144	
145	:::caution[Verify your restore path before you need it]
146	A backup you've never restored is a hope, not a plan. Do a restore into a
147	throwaway copy at least once so you know the bucket, credentials, and endpoint are
148	right before an incident forces the question.
149	:::

1 --- 2 title: Console screens 3 description: A visual tour of the Custos operator console — claim codes, accounts, devices, moderation, the audit log, transfers, and server status. 4 --- 5 6 A tour of the Custos operator console (the admin companion app). Every image here is 7 generated automatically from the app's own browser test harness across named scenarios, 8 including a degraded relay, so the pictures track the real UI and cannot quietly drift. 9 10 :::note[These are browser renders, not device captures] 11 These screenshots come from running the app frontend in a browser (the test harness), 12 not from an iPhone. Layout, copy, and states are faithful, but device-only details are 13 **not** pictured: the biometric (Face ID / Touch ID) gate that precedes every signing 14 action, the Secure Enclave-held admin key, camera QR scanning on the Pair screen, the 15 system share sheet, and iOS safe-area insets and font rendering. Treat these as accurate 16 diagrams, not pixel-exact device photos. 17 ::: 18 19 ## Home — mint a claim code 20 21 The console opens on the active relay, ready to mint a single-use, device-signed account 22 claim code. A **Relay federation** block up top reports whether the upstream relay is 23 actually crawling this server — status, exact events behind, last seen — with a 24 **Request crawl** re-invite (see 25 [Is the upstream relay seeing you?](/operator/running-a-relay/#is-the-upstream-relay-seeing-you)). 26 27 31 32 Before any relay is paired, the console asks you to pair this operator device. 33 34 38 39 ## Pairing 40 41 Pair a device with a relay by QR or manual entry. 42 43 47 48 ## Accounts 49 50 Every account on one relay, searchable by handle or DID, with a per-row blob-quota 51 readout. 52 53 57 58 ## Claim codes 59 60 The claim-code inventory splits live credentials from terminal history. 61 62 66 67 ## Devices 68 69 Every admin device registered on one relay — active and revoked — with a remote revoke 70 for a lost device. 71 72 76 77 ## Moderation 78 79 Account takedown and restore, then credential revocation — each an armed, biometric-gated 80 destructive action. 81 82 86 87 ## Audit log 88 89 Every privileged operator action — takedowns, credential sweeps, code mints and 90 revokes, device pairings and revocations, transfer cancels, account repairs, 91 crawl requests — is durably recorded with the credential that signed it: the 92 master token or the specific paired device. The Audit screen browses the trail 93 reverse-chronologically, filterable by action, with per-event drill-in by actor 94 or subject. 95 96 100 101 ## Transfers 102 103 In-flight device transfers an operator can watch and cancel. 104 105 109 110 ## Server status 111 112 One relay's health as it reports it — version and uptime, account counts, blob and block 113 totals, firehose state, and background-sweep last-runs. 2	title: Configuration
3	description: The configuration and environment surface that tunes a deployment.
4	---
5	
6	A Custos deployment is configured through environment variables and a small set
7	of runtime settings. This page is the operator's map of that surface — the
8	knobs you'll actually set, with the context to set them safely. The exhaustive,
9	drift-proof inventory of every setting is the
10	[generated configuration reference](/operator/reference/config/), produced
11	directly from the server's configuration types.
12	
13	Some of these settings change what your server *advertises* to clients, not just
14	how it behaves: `describeServer` names the capabilities this deployment offers,
15	and clients enable features accordingly. See
16	[Capabilities](/operator/capabilities/) for which settings those are.
17	
18	## Secrets
19	
20	These are injected at runtime and never baked into the image:
21	
22	| Variable | Role |
23	| --- | --- |
24	| `EZPDS_SIGNING_KEY_MASTER_KEY` | Master key (64 hex chars = 32 bytes) — the AES-256-GCM key that encrypts all at-rest signing material: every account's repo signing key, the server's OAuth signing key, the JWT secret, and the node identity. |
25	| `EZPDS_ADMIN_TOKEN` | Bearer token guarding the admin/operator endpoints. |
26	
27	:::danger[The master key must never change out from under the database]
28	The master key **is** the AES-256-GCM key those secrets are encrypted with; it is
29	used directly. Changing the environment variable alone on a populated instance
30	makes all existing secrets undecryptable — the server fails to load account repo
31	signing keys, and repo writes break. **Losing it is unrecoverable.** So: store it
32	in a secret manager (agenix / sops / your platform's secret store) never in the
33	repository or the image, and back it up.
34	
35	If it's already lost or you suspect it's compromised, stop and follow the
36	[master-key disaster runbook](/operator/master-key-runbook/) rather than
37	improvising — the recovery order matters.
38	:::
39	
40	Rotation is supported, but only as a deliberate offline operation: the
41	`pds rewrap-master-key` subcommand re-encrypts every stored secret from the old
42	key to the new one in a single atomic transaction, with the server stopped. Old
43	and new keys are supplied via `EZPDS_REWRAP_OLD_MASTER_KEY` /
44	`EZPDS_REWRAP_NEW_MASTER_KEY` environment variables (never CLI arguments), a
45	wrong old key aborts with no writes, and only after the re-wrap succeeds do you
46	point `EZPDS_SIGNING_KEY_MASTER_KEY` at the new key and restart. Never rotate by
47	changing the environment variable alone.
48	
49	## Runtime
50	
51	| Variable | Role |
52	| --- | --- |
53	| `PORT` | Injected by the platform; the server binds it. |
54	| `EZPDS_PUBLIC_URL` | The externally reachable origin of the PDS. |
55	| `EZPDS_AVAILABLE_USER_DOMAINS` | Domains users may claim handles on. |
56	| `EZPDS_LABELER_WATCHED` | Comma-separated labeler DIDs to watch; hosted accounts they label are flagged on the operator console. Off (empty) by default — see [Moderation § Labeler watching](/operator/moderation/#labeler-watching--flagged-accounts). |
57

59	its type, default, and doc-comment — is in the
